title: The moon keeps the calendar
hook: most Buddhist holy days fall on full and new moons; dates move each year

segments.voice: Yesterday the great collections closed: one sorted by kind, one by number. Your line: by kind and by number. Today the festival year opens.

Ask a Buddhist friend in Sri Lanka or Thailand when Vesak is this year, and they might have to check. Not because they've forgotten. Because it moves, sometimes by weeks from one year to the next. For the early Buddhists, the calendar wasn't a grid on the wall. It was in the sky: full, half, new. For the next sixteen days, this path walks through the Buddhist year, and it starts, fittingly, with the moon.
screen: `WHEN IS VESAK THIS YEAR?` → `IT MOVES.` → `THE CALENDAR IN THE SKY.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's India, time was kept by the moon. A month ran from one full moon or new moon to the next. The texts show the monks gathering on the full moon and the new moon, and in time the half moons too. These are uposatha days, observance days. On the full and new moon, monks gather to recite their rules together, the patimokkha. Lay people come to the monastery, listen to teaching, and some keep extra precepts for the day. That rhythm still beats across much of the Buddhist world. In Sri Lanka, every full moon day, called poya, is a public holiday. The big festivals sit on particular full moons: Vesak on one, the first sermon on another, the end of the rains retreat on another. A lunar year of twelve months is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so the festivals slide earlier each year, and every few years an extra month pulls them back. The dates move; the moon stays the same. Not every tradition keeps the moon. Japan moved to the solar calendar in the eighteen-seventies, and Japanese temples now generally mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on fixed solar dates. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities generally keep the lunar dates. Different calendars, same stories. And one gift of keeping the moon: anyone, anywhere, can look up and know roughly where they are in the holy year.
screen: `MONTHS FROM MOON TO MOON.` · `UPOSATHA: THE OBSERVANCE DAYS.` · `THE FESTIVALS SLIDE, THEN RESET.` · then, large: `THE MOON KEEPS THE CALENDAR.`

segments.voice: Picture tonight's sky and the moon wherever it is in its cycle, and ask yourself whether it's waxing or waning; if you're not sure, that's fine. Then picture the next full moon, and how you might keep it as a quiet day: a little more stillness, a little more care.
uposatha. The Pali word for the observance day, kept on full and new moons, when most Buddhist holy days fall, so their dates move each year. Today's word.
Your line: look up, and know. The calendar is in the sky. That's day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Across the Theravada world, lay Buddhists visit temples on full-moon and new-moon uposatha days, often keeping eight precepts, and monks recite the patimokkha on the full and new moons.

Vesak.meaning: a full moon remembering the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing

uposatha.meaning: an observance day on the full, new or half moon

patimokkha.meaning: the monks' rules, recited together on moon days

poya.meaning: a full moon day in Sri Lanka, a public holiday

notes: Block G opens. Confirm Vinaya Mv 2 account that King Bimbisara suggested the monks gather on moon days as other ascetics did (trapdoor).
